items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I lived with Mrs. Huston, giving her a certain amount every week for my room and board.

ctx.x: whiskey. The detectives took all the soap powder they could find, any old dirty rags and garbage and put them in those barrels of malt or mash to make certain that it could not be used anymore. I never saw or heard anything of the Wades again.

I stayed in the apartment alone for a few days and at with the Hustons. Then Mrs. Huston's son said he was going back to the South where he could carry a gun and I lived with Mrs. Huston, giving her a certain amount every week for my room and board.

One day I was out walking with one of my distant cousins that lived downstairs who's name was June, and two other boys in the neighbourhood named George Burr and Theodore Means. A nice little woman who must have been about 28 years old stopped us and asked if we could sing. Then she told us that she was a social worker and organist at a Presbyterian church and she would like to form a quartet of 4 boys. She offered to give us piano lessons and teach us some religious songs. We accepted her offer and a few nights…
